Copyright, 1916, BY King Features Syndicate)
I have been meaning to tell you something about this interesting and rather loose-jointed city of Tucson in the southwestern desert and the country around and about. I am afraid we are having a little boom because we are so badly crowded that our Sunshine club has been sending out word that this would be a good year not to come here and little houses are popping up all over the place. However I am confident that we will never be another Miami because, after all, we have no sea—and even allowing for slip in the weather this Winter, Miami and all Florida south of a line drawn across the state above Palm Beach are usually hotter.

The weather really did slip for a few weeks—snow, twice, if you can imagine, and almost every day ice on the dogs drinking water for about three weeks.

We have nothing TO offer comparable to the luxury and excitement of the fast Florida resorts and most evenings the town is dark and the streets are quiet soon after the movies let out. Our race track runs only on Sunday afternoons and the steeds are quarter-horses and, as for table-games, I can report that since 1910, I have heard OF only two playrooms in town, both running on the sneak, one of which was fearlessly exposed by our press and put out of business. I never know what happened to the other.

The other day I read where George Dixon reported from Miami that wild extravaganza was rife and that the noisiest spenders were black-marketers and absolute scum. There has been nothing like that here and I doubt that we will be so honored by the saloon trash. We haven't the facilities for the kind OF entertainment that they like which is quirky for you considering that Tucson in the old days was a roaring camp.

We have MANY beautiful homes, but mostly our homes are on the modest, domestic side and I think you would be impressed by the gumption and resourcefulness of so many people of that class which government paternalists so loftily describe as "little." You drive along a dusty road pushed into the desert on the outskirts with little more effort than a once-over with a bulldozer and you see where families are living in tents or trailers and putting up little houses, sometimes with the mother and children helping the dad who may be holding a job somewhere and working on his own house after hours.

Charles W. Herbert, Hollywood and newsreel camera man, who spent years traveling around the world doing movie features called "The Magic Carpet" and "Going Places," has a knack of finding such pioneers and doing their stories. A veteran of the first war, he was living here when Pearl Harbor happened, joined up as a lieutenant in the Signal Corps and served in the Aleutians and at Anzio. Last year, soon after he was discharged as captain, he discovered a man making a home of tamped earth, which means that he was shoveling soil into wooden forms and packing it down with an iron lamp on a stake. Recently, he came on a family of six from Michigan, parents and four children, whose story, briefly, is this:

The man's back was hurt in a farm accident and he was paralyzed for a time but recovered. His wife said that when he brought home his first pay they started a saving spree instead of a spending spree and when the doctor said they ought to come to this climate for the health of one of the children they bought a trailer and landed in the desert on the outskirts of Tucson. They paid $3.50 for an acre with water and sanitation, bought a lot of cement blocks and built a house entirely themselves, including the plumbing and wiring and the roof. Material cost them $780.

Mr. Herbert is that kind, himself. He could make his own house if he hadn't one already and most of this last year he has been doing just about that in remodeling and fitting an old building in town for a commercial photographic studio. In picture stories he does about the same that Ernie Pyle did in words when Ernie was rolling across our country discovering America and Americans before he went to war.

Housing, of course, is terribly expensive but, as I say, I see more building here than I observe anywhere else coming down across the country. They are using hardly any adobe now and going in for cement blocks, instead. A small, standing house that cost $500 a few years ago, sold for $500 recently and a $1,900 house went for $4,000, but there are still others who pull up and rough it a while and presently are seen at work with pick and shovel ditching in the desert for the foundations and then busy with the trowel and hammer.

And next year, maybe roses round the door.

Started last September by seven 12-to-15 year old boys, the workshop was built with donated scrap lumber, which the boys first stored under big lean-to, while they prepared the foundation for their shop. The boys worked hard through the inclement fall weather in an attempt to get the side-walls and roof up before the first snow. Eventually the number of boys dwindled to only two, but these plugged away, and by Christmas Eve the shop was ready for interior work.

The first completed project was an electric driven scroll saw which was built for less than $5 from a purchased blueprint, and which works very well. Plaques, initialed book-ends, knitting bag handles and other articles are in the making at the present time. As it is necessary for the boys to earn the amount of their light bill each month, they are accepting orders for articles.

tape ana Qelay. But the farther We get
from this part of the North American
continent, the harder it is to travel
either from or into the United States


II you want to take a trip south of
the Rio Grande and see something of
the other American republics, you must
first get United States passport In
the language of official travel guides,
this resembles "a small green-covered
notebook the first three pages
containing a photograph and descrip-
ton of the bearer. The remainder of
the pages left blank for visas"
And there are enough of these blank
pages to make up good scrapbook.
The passport takes some time-and some
trouble to obtain and costs $40. But
it is after you have got it that the
trouble really begins with vengeance.


First, you have to apply for the proper
forms on which to request visa from
the consulate of each country you want
to visit. Sometimes you're required to
appear in person, and getting to a con-
sulate is not always an easy trick if
you're starting from the Midwest or
South, or from small town. Then
you fill out these forms-lots and lots
of forms, different ones for every
country.


Depending on the country you're going
to visit, it may also be necessary for the
consul to cable (at your expense) his
Department of Foreign Affairs for au-
thority to issue your visa. Again-it
may take weeks. Nobody knows exactly
why that's done. 1t just is. After that,
you may have to pay visa fee: $3.50
for Bolivia; for Chile, $3.50 if you're
on business, $1.70 if you're tourist;
$3.50 for Uruguay, etc. How these par
ticular sums were arrived at is any
body's guess, but no two of them are
alike.


Numerous Photos Needed.


When you are getting vlsas, you have
to supply photographs. Visas for a
business trip to all parts of South and
Central America, for instance, require
10 photographs, and 13 of these-no
more, no less-have to be taken in pro-
file for our friends in Venezuela. The
number required for a pleasure trip is
not quite so large, but you had still
better put in stock of fullfaces and
profileS before you start your rounds.


After you have filed your application
and your photographs and have got
your visas, you still haven't complied
with the necessary red tape. Twenty
two of the countries in the Western
Hemisphere require that you have a
health certificate; 20 require smallpox
or vaccination certificate in addition,
and 10. a police certifiacte of good
conduct.


OF course, any one could manage to
get health and vaccination certificates,
and in most cases no check is ever made
as to whether they have been given by
a doctor. Any one without criminal
record can get q police certificate,
frequently from a bewildered chief of
police who never heard of such thing.
ANY one with serious police record
wouldn't get a passport, anyway.


Leaving Also Involved.


But your troubles are not over after
you have actually got into the countries
you wish to visit. There are still all
sorts of red tape about getting out AS

throw."

NEW YORK, Oct. 12.—Bernard M. Baruch tonight called on the United States to champion the principles of freedom, which he termed the formula of victory and survival, and to resist pressure to forsake democracy.

Mr. Baruch, United States delegate to the United Nations Atomic Energy Commission, said in address during the twentieth anniversary dinner of the College of the City of New York:

"We must bring reassurance to those countries where there is real and existing fear of freedom. It is to be seen in the disposition toward paternalism, in which thought and action flow from a higher level than the people themselves.

Security must come from within. It can never last if it comes from the top down; it must rise from the bottom."

Concerned With World Affairs.
He said that anything that happens anywhere is of deep concern to us—"the world can no longer be partitioned or put into separate compartments or even spheres."

He then turned to domestic problems with this statement:
"The issues as regards this country must be settled, and by ourselves, with no pressure from without or stimulation from false friends within our ranks.

Many light thinkers cry out for change. We are beseeched, cajoled, threatened, to alter our form of government—to elevate the state unto a mastery of the individual—to give us the priceless right of free speech, of free thought, or free religion, of free initiative, of free opportunity.

But the human being is more than a mere physical mechanism—it is more than a cog in the wheels of observation—disclosures of the right or of the left."

Tests Of Freedom Listed.

Mr. Baruch said that we rule in democracies not by violence but by consent and that changes are accomplished by the exercise of free will, not by guns, not by imprisonment, not by secret police, not by force.

He listed the following as tests of freedom:

I. Is there the right to free expression of opinions and of opposition and criticism of the government of the day?

II. Have the people the right to turn out government of which they disapprove, and are constitutional means provided by which they can make their will apparent?

III. Are there courts of justice, free from violence by the executive and free of all threats of mob violence and all association with any particular political parties?

IV. Do these courts administer open and well-established laws which are associated in the human mind with the broad principles of decency and justice?

V. Will there be fair play for poor as well as for rich, for private persons as well as Government officials?

VI. Will the rights of the individual, subject to his duties to the state, be maintained and asserted and exalted?

VII. Is the ordinary peasant or workman, carrying on his daily toil and striving to bring up a family, free from the fear that some grim police organization, under the control of a single party like the Gestapo started by the Nazis and Fascist parties, will tap him on the shoulder and pack him off, without fair or open trial, to bondage or ill treatment?"

~ desirable characteristic. By it


men are spurred on to higher
achievements. 1t constitutes an up
lifting influence which benefits not
only the individual but all mankind.
But ambition which is directed
towards selfish ends and for person.
al gain may lead to the depths OF deg
radiation. 1t is apt to result in un-
regulated and unrestrained efforts to
attain preferment and power. Still
vividly fresh in the thought of man.
kind is the example of mad ambition
which precipitated worldwide
war with its suffering, turmoil, and
bewilderment.


Because ambition is an inherent
characteristic of men, it must be
understood if it is to be rightly
directed. Just as "hope springs
eternal in the human breast" so does
the desire to progress. Recognition
of this, combined with the humility
which seeks divine guidance, will
eventually produce world citizens of
such integrity that tyranny and
dictatorship will vanish from our
midst. The power that true ambi-
ton acquires will promote peace and
advance the true brotherhood of
man.


Mary Baker Eddy, the Discoverer
and Founder of Christian Science,
and the author of its textbook,
Science and Health with Key to the
Scriptures" says in her Message to
The Mother Church for 1902 Up. -,
at does not follow that power must
mature into oppression; indeed, right
is the only real potency; and the
only true ambition is to serve God
